## Only Verified Work Becomes Progress

Verification is necessary for any agentic system. Agents create plans, summaries, memories, tests, patches, tool results, and claims that can later be mistaken for reliable state. A single agent can build on its own unverified outputs; a multi-agent system can multiply the problem by producing many such artifacts in parallel and passing them across workers. The central multi-agent question is therefore not only whether an output looks correct, but whether it is allowed to cross from private attempt into shared progress.

This is the admission problem in multi-agent systems. The mechanisms above can create more attempts, more diversity, more critique, more memory, and more branches. Those mechanisms become useful only when candidate work passes through a disciplined loop:

```text
spawn or search -> create artifacts -> verify -> prune, rank, or merge -> refine
```

@fig-loop turns this admission problem into the basic loop for structured test-time computation.

![Admission loop for structured test-time computation. Extra agents create value only when candidate work is turned into artifacts, verified, pruned or merged, and then admitted into shared state or escalated for review.](figures/test-time-computation-loop.svg){#fig-loop width=100% fig-alt="Loop diagram showing search expansion, artifact creation, verification, prune or merge, state update, and decision or escalation."}

The important threshold is admission. Search without verification adds plausible noise. Verification without search may miss alternatives. Multi-agent systems are powerful when they couple the two in settings where agents create non-redundant candidates and credible validators can reject bad ones. Agents can explore different evidence, hypotheses, code paths, tools, memories, or solution strategies, while the system uses tests, retrieval checks, formal constraints, human review, or cross-validation to decide what is pruned, ranked for review, merged, remembered, or escalated.

Artifact gates have levels. Conversational self-report and consensus are weakest: they can diagnose intent, but they do not by themselves inspect the environment or artifact. Model or rubric judges are useful for fuzzy outputs, but MASLab and visual-web work show that evaluator choice and judge design matter [@visualwebarena; @multiagentbench; @maslab]. Exact answer and state checks are stronger when the target state is compact, as in GAIA, tau-bench, and AndroidWorld [@gaia; @taubench; @androidworld]. Executable final-state validators are stronger still, as in WebArena, OSWorld, WorkArena, and SWE-bench [@webarena; @osworld; @workarena; @swebench]. Patch/test validation and candidate selection appear in Agentless and CAID [@agentless; @caid]. The stronger the downstream effect of an artifact, the stronger the gate should be: weak judges may be acceptable for ranking low-risk drafts, but artifacts that enter shared state, mutate files, call tools, or trigger irreversible actions need tests, provenance, permissions, or human escalation.

Artifacts are the selection surface for multi-agent search. They make partial work inspectable, replayable, comparable, and mergeable, so additional agents can be selected by evidence rather than by conversational confidence. Artifact-centered design can also strengthen single-agent and non-agentic baselines: Agentless resolves 96 of 300 SWE-bench Lite tasks at low reported cost through localization, sampled patches, generated reproduction tests, regression tests, and voting [@agentless]. The multi-agent claim is narrower: artifacts become especially valuable when they let parallel attempts remain isolated until evidence supports admission.

Different domains expose different admission boundaries. In software, useful artifacts include diffs, tests, failing traces, passing logs, issue-localization notes, dependency graphs, branch histories, review comments, and merge records. In scientific-agent work, useful artifacts include experiment plans, generated code, run logs, datasets, statistical outputs, reviewer rubrics, and replication traces. In document work, useful artifacts include structured edits, validation reports, provenance, and reversible transformations. In safety work, useful artifacts include permission manifests, tool-call logs, attack traces, policy decisions, and escalation records.

Artifacts matter because they can be inspected, replayed, compared, merged, or rejected. A message saying "the bug is fixed" is weak. A patch with a failing test before and a passing test after is stronger, though tests remain incomplete. A memory saying "the user prefers X" is weak. A memory entry with source, timestamp, update rule, and deletion policy is stronger, though memory can still preserve false assumptions. A debate transcript claiming consensus is weak. A set of independent solutions plus a deterministic verifier is stronger.

CAID is a concrete positive example in software engineering. It uses asynchronous delegation, isolated worktrees, centralized task assignment, and branch-and-merge integration [@caid]. On PaperBench, CAID improves MiniMax 2.5 from 10.4% to 36.7% and Claude 4.5 Sonnet from 57.2% to 63.3% in the reported setup; on Commit0-Lite, it also improves Claude from 53.1% to 59.1%. The key move is not just having more coding agents. It is letting parallel work remain private until commits, tests, git history, and manager review provide enough evidence to merge. @fig-caid shows the branch-and-merge workflow. The caveat is equally important: soft isolation can underperform, and the best number of engineers depends on task modularity and manager quality.

![CAID branch-and-merge workflow for asynchronous software-engineering agents. A manager decomposes tasks, engineers work in isolated git worktrees, and completed commits are verified, merged, and used to update later delegation. Reproduced from @caid.](figures/caid-multi-agent-teaser.pdf){#fig-caid width=92% fig-alt="CAID teaser diagram showing asynchronous multi-agent software engineering with isolated worktrees, delegation, verification, and merge."}

Scientific-agent systems show the same admission problem at a larger scale. The AI Scientist, AI co-scientist, Agent Laboratory, Curie, InternAgent, MLGym, and related systems point toward agentic research workflows that generate hypotheses, write code, run experiments, and review outputs [@aiscientist; @aicoscientist; @agentlaboratory; @curie; @internagent; @mlgym]. PaperBench evaluates whether agents can replicate AI research, pushing evaluation toward the full artifact chain rather than a single answer [@paperbench]. AgentRxiv adds a shared archive for agent-generated research reports, illustrating how scientific collaboration can become asynchronous artifact retrieval rather than direct conversation [@agentrxiv]. @aiscientistsdontreason provide an important caution: producing outputs that look like scientific work is not the same as reasoning scientifically. Curie is useful here because it makes experimental rigor, workflow validation, and structured experiment records part of the system rather than leaving them implicit [@curie]. For scientific agents, the gate must include replication, statistical validity, provenance, novelty checks, and expert review.

The artifact-centered view also explains a plausible near-term pattern visible in scientist-in-the-loop and co-pilot systems: human-governed portfolios of agent attempts [@aicoscientist; @agentlaboratory]. The claim is not that fully autonomous agent organizations are already reliable. It is that humans can supply decomposition, taste, accountability, escalation, and final merge judgment while agents expand the search frontier. This is the practical scaling argument for multi-agent systems: one human can supervise more hypotheses, patches, experiments, reviews, and alternatives when the system keeps attempts isolated, evidence-rich, and mergeable. The bottleneck becomes integration quality and review bandwidth, not raw generation; artifact gates are therefore also compression and selection mechanisms.

Durable artifacts are therefore the medium through which test-time search becomes inspectable progress. But admission is not the end of coordination. Once artifacts, memories, logs, and tool results become shared context, they shape the next round of work. The next problem is whether the accumulating shared state remains coherent, truthful, safe, and repairable.
